chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
title: Nat Cole building himself as a singer and hiding his piano
summary: Collins understood Nat was building Nat Cole; on stage he got no solos, and Collins urged him to let the public see his piano playing.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: No, I don't remember him firing anybody. Everybody quit when he got -- you know, ready to leave. But Nat was a very nice individual, very easy going. Oh, he was very nice. I admired him very much. And as I said, you know, about my not taking solos and all that, it was -- if I didn't want to stay there, if I didn't have reason for being there, I should have quit myself. It wasn't -- I could understand what he was doing. He's building Nat Cole, you know. No matter how he felt about me or how he felt about my playing, and the mere fact that I was there, I knew that he admired my playing because we would get together after the job and really get into playing and really do some beautiful things.
But on stage, no, it was Nat Cole.

Yeah, I know; that's funny, isn't it, but this is the way it was. Now, he got to the point where he didn't even want to play because he didn't want to be identified as a musician. As great as he was, he stopped

Well, offstage he would -- you know, we would get -- yeah, we'd still play. But I mean as far as the public is concerned. There were a lot of youngsters who didn't realize what a great pianist Nat was. And I would get him -- sometimes we'd get in these discussions, I'd tell him look, you're foolish. I mean, you want to be a stand up singer like Sinatra. Sinatra wishes he could play piano. I mean, you've got two shots, you've got to let these people know how versatile you are. So he finally started playing, but he never let me play.
But as I said, it was up to me to either leave or stay, you know, because I knew what his policy was, I knew what he was driving at, and if I didn't like I should have left. But --
